w: Roman soldiers held this fort on the Stanegate for nearly three centuries, guarding the road south of Hadrian's Wall before the Wall even existed. Excavations here turned up the Vindolanda tablets - Britain's oldest surviving handwritten documents, letters home from a frontier nobody wanted posting to.
s: Roman fort that yielded Britain's oldest handwriting
_facts: Roman auxiliary fort south of Hadrian's Wall, occupied c. 85-370 AD
Guarded the Stanegate road from the Tyne to the Solway Firth
Noted for the Vindolanda tablets, oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain at time of discovery

w: Newcastle and Gateshead have been laced together by this arch since 1928, when George V cut the ribbon on what became Tyneside's defining silhouette. The same engineering firm, Mott, Hay and Anderson, later built the Forth Road Bridge - but the Tyne came first, four years before Sydney Harbour borrowed the look.
s: The arch Sydney Harbour Bridge borrowed its look from
_facts: Through arch bridge linking Newcastle and Gateshead over the River Tyne
Designed by Mott, Hay and Anderson, built by Dorman Long
Opened 10 October 1928 by King George V; tenth tallest structure in Newcastle

w: A loop of the River Coquet cradles this ruined stronghold, first documented in 1157 and fought over for two centuries by Scots raiders, King John's court and the Percy family. It survived Scottish sieges in 1327, hosted a king overnight, and still broods over the Northumberland coast a mile from the sea.
s: Ruined riverside castle that outlasted Scottish sieges
_facts: Ruined medieval castle occupying a loop of the River Coquet, less than a mile from the coast
First documented 1157-1164; King John stayed overnight in 1213
Besieged twice by the Scots in 1327 without success; later held by the Percy family

w: Behind Alnwick Castle's formal cascades lurks a walled enclosure the Duchess of Northumberland planted on purpose with over 100 toxic, intoxicating and narcotic species - the Poison Garden, added in 2005 and still the reason a botanical garden makes headlines. The revival wasn't short on controversy either.
s: The Duchess's walled garden of 100+ toxic plants
_facts: Formal gardens adjacent to Alnwick Castle, revived from disrepair from 2001
A Poison Garden with over 100 toxic, intoxicating and narcotic plants was added in Feb 2005
12th Duke of Northumberland donated the site and 9 million pounds toward costs; sparked public disputes

w: Twin monasteries founded in 674 and 684, on the Wear and the Tyne, became one of early medieval Europe's great centres of learning - producing the Venerable Bede. Vikings sacked it, the Normans briefly revived it, and Henry VIII finished the job in 1536, leaving Grade I ruins beside two working parish churches.
s: Ruined double monastery that produced the Venerable Bede
_facts: Benedictine double monastery founded 674-5 (St Peter's) and 684-5 (St Paul's Jarrow)
Became a centre of learning that produced Bede
Sacked by Vikings, abandoned, refounded as cells of Durham Priory, dissolved 1536; both churches survive as Grade I listed parish churches

w: Perched on a mile-long crag of the Whin Sill, this is the best-preserved fort on Hadrian's Wall and was called its "grandest station" - occupied for nearly 300 years and now looking down on some of the emptiest hills in England. Finds from the site sit in its own museum, plus two more in Newcastle and at Chesters.
s: Hadrian's Wall's "grandest station," on a crag
_facts: Auxiliary fort on Hadrian's Wall at Housesteads, occupied almost 300 years
Called the "grandest station" on the Wall, one of best-preserved and most extensively displayed
Now owned by National Trust, cared for by English Heritage; finds shown in site museum plus museums in Newcastle and Chesters

w: A fortified manor rather than a true castle, Aydon sits near Corbridge with the defensive walls of a border stronghold and the domestic comforts of a gentry house underneath. Scheduled as an ancient monument and listed Grade I, it's the kind of place built by people who wanted both safety and a decent parlour.
s: Fortified manor house near Corbridge, Grade I listed
_facts: Fortified manor house at Aydon near Corbridge, Northumberland, sometimes called Aydon Hall
Scheduled Ancient Monument and Grade I listed building

w: Long before Hadrian's Wall was planned, this Roman road already linked the crossings at Corbridge and Carlisle, running through the gap between the Tyne and Irthing valleys. Unlike most Roman roads it wanders with the land rather than punching straight through - and a stretch is still a working lane today.
s: The Roman road that pre-dates Hadrian's Wall
_facts: Roman road and frontier linking Corstopitum (Corbridge) and Luguvalium (Carlisle)
Predated Hadrian's Wall by several decades; the Wall later followed a similar route
Unusually followed easy gradients rather than a straight path; a section survives as a minor road between Fourstones and Vindolanda

w: A lone peel tower crowning a crag above the Scottish Borders, built for defence in centuries when this frontier meant Border Reivers and Scots-English raiding. Now a Scheduled Ancient Monument, it holds a five-star VisitScotland rating shared by only eight other sites in the country.
s: Border peel tower on a crag, five-star rated
_facts: Peel tower at Smailholm, atop Lady Hill crag, near Kelso in the Scottish Borders
Scheduled Ancient Monument in care of Historic Environment Scotland
Awarded maximum five-star VisitScotland tourist attraction status in 2007, one of only nine sites in Scotland with that rating

w: Built in 1364 in a bold H-shape with a tower on each corner, Langley burned in 1405 and then sat in ruins for five hundred years - abandoned long enough that its 1914 restoration counted as a resurrection. It now runs as a hotel, so you can sleep inside walls that once stood empty for centuries.
s: 14th-century tower house, ruined then reborn as a hotel
_facts: Medieval tower house near Haydon Bridge, Northumberland, Grade I listed
Built in 1364 in an H-shape with four corner towers
Severely damaged by fire in 1405, left in ruins for 500 years, restored in 1914, now operates as a hotel

w: Newcastle's science and history museum holds the wreck of a legend: Turbinia, the first steam turbine ship, which stunned onlookers by outrunning every vessel at the 1897 Spithead Navy Review. Built in 1894 by Charles Parsons, she set the template every warship afterward would follow.
s: Home to Turbinia, the ship that outran the Navy in 1897
_facts: Science and local history museum in Blandford Square, Newcastle, managed by North East Museums
Displays Turbinia, first steam turbine-powered ship, built 1894 by Charles Algernon Parsons
Turbinia was demonstrated dramatically at the Spithead Navy Review in 1897, then the fastest ship in the world

w: A modest Hadrian's Wall fort known to Rome as Brocolitia, a 3.5-acre posting whose name may simply mean "badger holes" in the old Celtic tongue. It turns up in a 5th-century Roman register as Procolita and a 7th-century document as Brocoliti - a small garrison that still left a paper trail across centuries.
s: Wall fort whose name may just mean "badger holes"
_facts: Site of a 3.5-acre auxiliary fort on Hadrian's Wall called Brocolitia/Procolita/Brocolita
Name appears in the 5th-century Notitia Dignitatum and 7th-century Ravenna Cosmography
Name likely Celtic, possibly translating to 'badger holes'

w: Seat of the Dukes of Northumberland since the Norman Conquest, remodelled again and again until it became one of England's grandest Grade I piles - and, paired with its adjoining garden, pulls over 600,000 visitors a year. The Percy family still lives here; you're stepping into their actual home.
s: The Percy family's actual home since the Conquest
_facts: Castle and country house built following the Norman Conquest, renovated and remodelled repeatedly
Grade I listed, seat of Ralph Percy, 12th Duke of Northumberland and family
Received over 600,000 visitors a year in 2016 combined with the adjacent Alnwick Garden

w: The world's first tilting bridge opened in 2001, rotating its whole arch upward like an eyelid to let river traffic pass beneath - hence the nicknames Blinking Eye and Winking Eye. Award-winning and instantly iconic, it links Gateshead's arts quarter to Newcastle's Quayside with a wink rather than a ramp.
s: The 'Blinking Eye' - world's first tilting bridge
_facts: Pedestrian and cyclist tilt bridge over the River Tyne linking Gateshead and Newcastle Quayside
First tilting bridge ever constructed; opened to the public in 2001
Designed by WilkinsonEyre and Gifford; nicknamed the 'Blinking Eye' or 'Winking Eye' Bridge

w: Perched at around 1,000 feet in the North Pennines, Alston shares the title of highest market town in England with Buxton - a former lead, zinc and coal mining hub whose conservation-area centre still stands on old mining money. Isolated even by Pennine standards, you reach it on purpose, not by accident.
s: England's highest market town, an old mining hub
_facts: Town in Cumbria at about 1,000 feet, shares title of 'highest market town in England' with Buxton
Historic centre for mining lead, zinc, iron, copper and coal
Town centre largely a designated conservation area with several listed buildings, historically in Cumberland

w: Thomas of Lancaster built this coastal fortress in the 1310s as a refuge should his rebellion against Edward II go wrong - it did, and he was captured fleeing toward it before execution. John of Gaunt later strengthened it against the Scots, and it changed hands often in the Wars of the Roses before falling to ruin.
s: Coastal ruin built as a rebel earl's last refuge
_facts: 14th-century fortification on the Northumberland coast between Craster and Embleton
Built 1313-1322 by Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster, opposed to Edward II; Thomas captured near the castle in 1322 and executed
Expanded by John of Gaunt in the 1380s against Scottish threat; changed hands repeatedly in the Wars of the Roses

w: Fifteen to twenty islands off the Northumberland coast, depending on how the tide sits, split by Staple Sound into an Inner and an Outer group. Inner Farne barely clears the waves at 19 metres, Staple Island a little higher at 14 - a low, scattered archipelago that all but disappears and reappears with the sea.
s: A scattered archipelago that shifts with the tide
_facts: Group of 15-20 islands off the Northumberland coast, split into Inner and Outer groups by Staple Sound
Highest point on Inner Farne is 19 metres, on Staple Island 14 metres above sea level
Part of the civil parish of North Sunderland

w: Founded in 1091 alongside the castle it takes its cue from, rebuilt after an 1216 fire and finished by 1350, Newcastle's Grade I cathedral is best known for the lantern spire crowning its tower - a 15th-century flourish visible for miles. It only became a cathedral in 1882, seat of the Bishop of Newcastle ever since.
s: Cathedral famed for its 15th-century lantern spire
_facts: Cathedral Church of St Nicholas, Church of England, Grade I listed, founded 1091
Original Norman church destroyed by fire in 1216; current building completed 1350
Tower noted for 15th-century lantern spire; raised to cathedral status in 1882
